body:
How Buddha sculpture developed before and during the Guptas

The Mathura and Sarnath schools are 2 important traditions of Indian stone sculpture. Both contributed to the development of the Buddha image, but they are recognised through different materials and ways of representing the human form.

Human images of the Buddha became increasingly important during the early centuries CE. Before this development, many Buddhist reliefs represented his presence through symbols such as the Bodhi tree, an empty throne or the Dharma wheel. The growth of human Buddha images did not eliminate these earlier symbols; both types of representation continued to be used.

Mathura was already a major sculptural centre during the Kushana period, particularly from the 1st to the 3rd centuries CE. Its artistic tradition continued and developed under the Guptas. Sarnath became especially celebrated for refined Buddha images of the Gupta period, including major works of the 5th century CE.

It is therefore wrong to identify every Mathura Buddha as Kushana or to assume that the Mathura school disappeared when Gupta rule began. The names of artistic schools refer primarily to distinctive sculptural traditions associated with particular centres.

Mathura: Sandstone, bodily volume and visible drapery

The Mathura school is associated with red or mottled red sandstone. Its Buddha images typically display a strong physical presence. Many have broad shoulders, full bodily forms, rounded facial features and a prominent halo behind the head.

The robe may cling to the body while its folds remain clearly indicated. In important Gupta-period Mathura images, these folds can appear as raised, narrow lines across the garment. The overall form remains substantial, even as the features become more refined and serene.

The seated Buddha from the Katra Mound at Mathura, dating to the 2nd century CE, is a useful earlier example of the tradition. It belongs to the Kushana period, not the Gupta period. The Buddha is seated with crossed legs in padmasana and raises the right hand in abhaya mudra, the gesture of reassurance or freedom from fear.

This Kushana example provides a foundation for recognising the fuller bodily treatment associated with the Mathura tradition. The sculptors of the Gupta period developed greater refinement while preserving several recognisable regional features.

Sarnath: Refined proportions and nearly transparent robes

The Sarnath school is especially associated with a restrained and delicate representation of the Buddha. Gupta-period images from this centre commonly use the fine, light-coloured sandstone associated with Chunar, near Varanasi.

The Buddha's body is generally slender and well proportioned. The face is calm, the eyes are often half-closed, and the outlines are soft and rhythmically controlled. One of the most distinctive features is the treatment of the monastic robe. It appears extremely thin and closely fitted, with folds that may be almost invisible.

This treatment creates the impression of a transparent or nearly transparent drapery. In contrast to the more visibly patterned folds of many Mathura images, the Sarnath robe becomes visually integrated with the surface of the body.

The seated preaching Buddha at Sarnath

A celebrated Buddha image from Sarnath, generally dated to the late 5th century CE, shows the Buddha seated in padmasana with the hands arranged in Dharmachakrapravartana mudra.

Dharmachakrapravartana mudra is the hand gesture associated with the Buddha's first sermon. The image can also be identified through the sculptural panel beneath the seat, where a wheel appears with deer on either side and figures representing disciples.

These features connect the sculpture to the historical and religious significance of Sarnath. The combination of a preaching gesture, wheel and deer makes the identification more reliable than judging the image from facial appearance alone.

Mathura and Sarnath compared

FeatureMathura schoolSarnath school
Important centreMathura, Uttar PradeshSarnath, Uttar Pradesh
Characteristic stoneRed or mottled red sandstoneFine light-coloured Chunar sandstone
Body treatmentFuller and more strongly modelledSlender, balanced and softly modelled
RobeFolds often visibly indicatedThin, clinging drapery with minimal visible folds
Important exampleGupta-period standing BuddhaLate 5th-century seated preaching Buddha
Recognisable gestureAbhaya mudra in important Buddha examplesDharmachakrapravartana mudra in the celebrated preaching Buddha

The comparison identifies typical tendencies, not inflexible rules. Both centres produced different kinds of images, and individual sculptures may not display every characteristic associated with their school. Material, form, gesture, date and findspot should be considered together.

Important distinctions between monuments at Sarnath

Sarnath appears in both Mauryan and Gupta art, but the monuments belong to different periods. The Ashokan Lion Capital belongs to the 3rd century BCE and is a pillar capital made under Mauryan patronage. The celebrated seated preaching Buddha belongs to the late 5th century CE and represents the Gupta sculptural tradition.

Likewise, the 2nd-century CE Katra Mound Buddha is a Kushana-period example from Mathura, while important standing Buddha images continued to be produced at Mathura during the Gupta period in the 5th century CE. The period of a particular sculpture must be identified separately from the longer history of its artistic centre.

Viewed together, the chronology of this lesson runs from Mauryan pillars and the early Sanchi stupa in the 3rd century BCE, through post-Mauryan developments in stupa architecture and Mathura sculpture, to Gupta temples and refined Buddha images of the 5th and early 6th centuries CE. These developments were connected, but they were not simultaneous creations of one dynasty.

Prelims focus

  • Mathura is associated with red sandstone, fuller forms and more visibly indicated garment folds.
  • Sarnath Gupta sculpture is associated with Chunar sandstone, refined proportions and thin, clinging drapery.
  • The Katra Mound seated Buddha at Mathura belongs to the Kushana period, around the 2nd century CE.
  • The celebrated preaching Buddha at Sarnath belongs to the late 5th century CE.
  • Abhaya mudra expresses reassurance; Dharmachakrapravartana mudra is associated with the first sermon.
  • Trap: The Sarnath Lion Capital is Mauryan, while the famous seated preaching Buddha from Sarnath is Gupta.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, printed pp. 48–49 and 52–53; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Buddhism and Buddhist Art, section on Gupta images at Mathura and Sarnath, consulted 23 November 2026; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, collection record 1979.6, Standing Buddha Offering Protection, Mathura, late 5th century, consulted 23 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Buddha in Different Mudras, Dharmachakrapravartana image at Sarnath Museum, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Gupta-period Mathura Buddha in red sandstone, with full bodily forms, visible robe folds, a surviving halo and a missing right hand.
pictures.caption: Gupta-period Mathura sculpture often uses red sandstone and clearly modelled bodily form.

data.description: Authentic photograph of the Met’s Standing Buddha Offering Protection (1979.6), Mathura, late 5th century CE. Show the full red-sandstone sculpture, surviving halo, strong bodily modelling and visible garment folds. Preserve the missing right hand.

pictures.alt: Sarnath’s seated Buddha displays the sermon gesture and a delicate robe, with a halo behind the head and a wheel, deer and disciples beneath the seat.
pictures.caption: The late 5th-century Sarnath Buddha is associated with the first sermon and Dharmachakrapravartana mudra.

data.description: Frontal photograph of the actual Sarnath Museum Buddha: Chunar sandstone, late 5th century CE; halo, half-closed eyes, slender body, thin clinging robe, padmasana and Dharmachakrapravartana mudra. Include the full base with wheel, deer and disciples.
data.source_hint: Sarnath Museum, Uttar Pradesh; use a clear photograph of the original sculpture.

title: Gupta Buddha Sculpture: Distinguishing the Mathura and Sarnath Schools
